content: An endometrial polyp, also known as a uterine polyp, is a growth or lesion that develops in the lining of the uterus, called the endometrium. These polyps occupy space within the uterine cavity and are relatively common, affecting up to 10% of women. They can either have a broad, flat base (sessile) or be attached to the uterine wall by a thin, elongated stalk (pedunculated). Pedunculated polyps are more frequently observed than sessile ones. The size of these polyps can vary significantly, ranging from just a few millimeters to several centimeters. In cases where the polyp is pedunculated, it may extend through the cervix and into the vagina. Additionally, small blood vessels are often present within polyps, particularly in larger ones. The exact cause of endometrial polyps remains unclear, but they are believed to be influenced by hormonal factors, particularly circulating estrogen, which stimulates their growth. Many polyps are asymptomatic, meaning they do not cause noticeable symptoms. However, when symptoms do occur, they may include irregular menstrual bleeding, bleeding between menstrual cycles, excessively heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia), and vaginal bleeding after menopause. Bleeding from the blood vessels within the polyp can contribute to increased blood loss during menstruation or cause spotting between periods or after menopause. If a polyp protrudes through the cervix into the vagina, it may result in pain, known as dysmenorrhea. Endometrial polyps can be diagnosed using various methods, including vaginal ultrasound (sonohysterography), hysteroscopy, and dilation and curettage (D&C). However, detection via ultrasonography can be challenging, especially in cases of endometrial hyperplasia, which is an abnormal thickening of the endometrium. Larger polyps may also be missed during curettage procedures. On imaging, a feeding blood vessel within the polyp may be visible using power Doppler ultrasound. Treatment for endometrial polyps typically involves surgical removal, which can be performed using curettage or hysteroscopy. During curettage, there is a risk of missing polyps, so the uterus may first be explored with grasping forceps to minimize this possibility. Hysteroscopy allows direct visualization of the polyp, which can then be removed through the cervix. If the polyp is large, it may need to be sectioned into smaller pieces for removal. In cases where cancerous cells are identified within the polyp, a hysterectomy (surgical removal of the uterus) may be recommended. However, if cancer is ruled out, a hysterectomy is generally not considered necessary. Regardless of the method used, polyp removal is typically performed under general anesthesia. Endometrial polyps are usually benign, but some may be precancerous or even cancerous. Approximately 0.5% of endometrial polyps contain adenocarcinoma cells. These polyps can also increase the risk of miscarriage in women undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF) treatment. If a polyp develops near the fallopian tubes, it may interfere with fertility and make it more difficult to conceive. While treatments like hysteroscopy are effective in removing the affected polyp, recurrence of endometrial polyps is relatively common. Endometrial polyps are most frequently observed in women in their 40s and 50s. The use of tamoxifen, a medication commonly prescribed for breast cancer, or hormone replacement therapy can also increase the likelihood of developing uterine polyps. Endometrial polyps are present in up to 10% of women and are found in approximately 25% of women who experience abnormal vaginal bleeding. Structurally, endometrial polyps may occur as solitary growths or in clusters. They are typically round or oval in shape and can range in size from a few millimeters to several centimeters in diameter. Their color is usually similar to the surrounding endometrium, appearing red or brown, although larger polyps may appear darker red. These polyps are composed of dense fibrous tissue (stroma), blood vessels, and gland-like spaces lined with endometrial epithelium. Pedunculated polyps are attached to the uterine wall by a thin stalk, while sessile polyps are connected by a broad, flat base. Pedunculated polyps are more commonly observed than sessile ones.
